title: Tech myths that won't die: 404, 640K, the space pen and Nuclear Gandhi
description: Room 404 at CERN, Bill Gates's 640K quote, NASA's million-dollar space pen, the Gandhi bug in *Civilization*, Grace Hopper finding the first bug. They're great stories, and they're mostly wrong. Each Question gives the popular version and asks what really happened. The Explanations show where each myth started and why it spread.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: Is the 404 error named after Room 404 at CERN, where the web's first servers supposedly sat?

options.text: No. Web pioneer Robert Cailliau says 404 was never linked to any room at CERN
Yes. Tim Berners-Lee's office was Room 404, and he was often out
Yes, but the room was a server closet, not an office
No. It is named after the fourth floor of the first web host in California

questions.explanation:
No room is involved. The story surfaced in the early 2000s: the first web servers lived in Room 404, Tim Berners-Lee worked there, and he was often "not found". It is neat, memorable, and wrong.

In 2017, Wired asked Robert Cailliau, who built the web with Berners-Lee at CERN, about it. His reply: "404 was never linked to any room or any physical place at CERN. That's a complete myth." Error codes were grouped into numeric ranges "according to the whims of the programmer", client errors landed in the 400s, and "not found" happened to get 404.

The myth has the shape that makes stories spread: a famous name, a specific detail (a room number), and a punchline. None of those make it evidence. Ask for the source of the specific detail, and this one has none.
questions.references: [Wired: Page not found — a brief history of the 404 error (2017)](https://www.wired.com/story/page-not-found-a-brief-history-of-the-404-error/)

questions.title: In an HTTP status code such as 404, what does the first digit 4 tell you?

options.text: The error is on the client's side: the request itself can't be fulfilled as sent
The server crashed or failed while handling a valid request
The resource has moved, and the client should look elsewhere
The request was retried four times before failing

questions.explanation:
HTTP status codes are three digits, and only the first one is a category. RFC 9110 defines five classes:

| First digit | Class | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1xx | Informational | Request received, continuing |
| 2xx | Successful | Request received, understood and accepted |
| 3xx | Redirection | Further action needed, such as following a new URL |
| 4xx | Client Error | The client seems to have erred |
| 5xx | Server Error | The server failed to perform a valid request |

A 404 says the server found nothing at the URL the client asked for. The server is working fine; the request pointed at something that isn't there. That is why a typo in a URL gets a 404, while a crashed database behind a correct URL should get a 500.

The RFC also says the last two digits "do not have any categorization role". 404 is not "error type 04" of anything. It is just the number that "not found" was given, which fits Cailliau's account of how the codes were picked.
questions.references: [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, §15 Status Codes](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-status-codes), [Wired: Page not found — a brief history of the 404 error (2017)](https://www.wired.com/story/page-not-found-a-brief-history-of-the-404-error/)

questions.title: Did Bill Gates say that "640K ought to be enough for anybody"?

options.text: There is no evidence he did, and he has denied it
Yes, at the IBM PC launch in 1981
Yes, in a 1981 interview with InfoWorld
Yes, but he meant it as a joke about MS-DOS

questions.explanation:
Nobody has found a recording, transcript or article from 1981 in which Gates says it. The quote usually comes with no date at all, or with "1981" attached because that is when the IBM PC shipped.

Gates addressed it in his newspaper column in 1996. He wrote that he had said "some stupid things and some wrong things, but not that", and complained that the quotation comes with no citation and just "floats like a rumor".

A denial alone doesn't prove anything; people misremember what they said. The stronger evidence is the paper trail. Quote Investigator, who searches old newspapers and magazines for the first appearance of famous quotes, found the line only years after 1981, and in a different form. The next Question looks at when.
questions.references: [Quote Investigator: 640K of computer memory is more than enough for anyone (2011)](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2011/09/08/640k-enough/)

questions.title: In what year did a version of the 640K quote first appear in print?
questions.explanation:
**1985**, four years after the IBM PC launched. On 29 April 1985, InfoWorld printed a line credited to Gates about setting the upper limit of PC-DOS at 640K and thinking "nobody would ever need that much memory". That is a different claim from the famous one. It says the designers underestimated demand, not that 640K would be enough forever.

The punchy wording, "640K ought to be enough for anyone", shows up in InfoWorld on 1 January 1990. By then it was a stock example in columns about bad tech predictions.

This is how many misquotes grow. A real but vague remark gets paraphrased, the paraphrase gets sharper each time it is retold, and a date is attached later to make it sound like a prediction. When a quote has no source from the year it was supposedly said, look for its first appearance in print. The gap between that year and the claimed one tells you a lot.
questions.references: [Quote Investigator: 640K of computer memory is more than enough for anyone (2011)](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2011/09/08/640k-enough/)

images.alt: A timeline of the 640K quote. 1981: supposedly said when the IBM PC launched, but no source from 1981 has been found. 1985: first in print, in InfoWorld on 29 April, as a line credited to Gates about setting PC-DOS's limit at 640K and thinking nobody would ever need that much memory. 1990: the famous wording, "640K ought to be enough for anyone", in InfoWorld on 1 January. 1996: Gates denies it in his newspaper column, saying the quote never has a citation and floats like a rumor.

questions.title: The IBM PC's Intel 8088 processor had 20 address lines, each carrying one bit of a memory address. How many kilobytes of memory could it address?
questions.description: 1 KB = 1,024 bytes. Answer with a whole number of kilobytes.
questions.explanation:
20 bits give 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 distinct addresses, one byte each. Divided by 1,024 bytes per kilobyte, that's **1,024 KB**, or 1 MB.

So why did 640 KB become the famous limit? When IBM designed the PC in 1981, it had to fit more than RAM into that 1 MB of addresses. Video cards need memory the processor can write to, and the BIOS and expansion cards need ROM. IBM placed all of these at the top of the address space, starting at address A0000 hex, which is 640 KB. That left 640 KB of contiguous addresses for RAM, known as **conventional memory**. The 384 KB above it is the **upper memory area**.

DOS programs expected their memory in that one block, so a PC could not simply add RAM above 640 KB and have programs use it. Later tricks such as expanded memory, extended memory and upper-memory loaders existed to work around a hardware layout, not around anyone's opinion of how much memory people needed.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Intel 8088](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel_8088), [Wikipedia: Conventional memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventional_memory), [Wikipedia: Upper memory area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_memory_area)

images.alt: A bar showing the IBM PC's 1,024 KB address space. The first 640 KB, from 0 to address A0000 hex, is RAM for DOS and programs, labeled conventional memory. The remaining 384 KB, the upper area, holds video memory from 640 to 768 KB, reserved space for adapter ROMs from 768 to 960 KB, and the BIOS from 960 KB up. A note says IBM put video memory and ROMs at the top in 1981, so RAM above 640 KB could not extend the block programs used.
images.caption: Simplified from the IBM PC memory map. Diagram drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: The story goes that NASA spent millions developing a pen that writes in space, while the Soviets used pencils. Who actually paid to develop the Fisher Space Pen?

options.text: Paul Fisher's pen company, with about $1 million of its own money
NASA, through a multimillion-dollar development contract
The U.S. Air Force, which later passed the design to NASA
NASA and the Soviet space agency, as a joint project

questions.explanation:
NASA didn't pay for the development. Paul C. Fisher and his company spent about $1 million of their own money on a pressurized ink cartridge. Pressurized nitrogen pushes the thick ink toward the ball, so the pen works without gravity, upside down, and in a wide temperature range.

NASA tested the pen and then bought it. In 1968 it ordered 400 of them for the Apollo program at $2.39 each, a bulk discount on the $3.98 list price. The photo shows Walter Cunningham writing in orbit during Apollo 7, in October 1968.

The joke works because it flatters a common suspicion: that big agencies waste money on problems a simple tool could solve. That suspicion wasn't baseless, as the next Question shows. But here the expensive research was private, and the pens were cheap.
questions.references: [Scientific American: Fact or fiction? NASA spent millions to develop a pen that would write in space (2006)](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-nasa-spen/), [Wikipedia: Space pen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_pen)

images.alt: Astronaut Walter Cunningham in a white flight suit inside the cramped Apollo 7 command module, head bent, writing on a notepad with a slim pen. A camera film magazine floats in the air near his hand.
images.caption: Walter Cunningham writing with a space pen on day nine of Apollo 7, 1968. NASA photo, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Astro-space-pen.jpg).

questions.title: "Why not just use a pencil?" Which of these were real reasons to keep pencils out of a spacecraft?

options.text: Broken tips and graphite dust float around in weightlessness instead of falling to the floor
Graphite conducts electricity, so floating fragments could get into electronics
Wood and graphite burn, which became a serious worry after the 1967 Apollo 1 fire
Pencils can't leave a mark without gravity pressing the lead onto the paper
Pencil marks fade quickly in the cabin's radiation

questions.explanation:
Pencils do write in orbit. The lead leaves a mark through friction as you press it against the paper, and your hand supplies that pressure, not gravity. Both American and Soviet crews used pencils early on.

The problems came from what pencils leave behind. On Earth, a snapped tip or graphite dust falls to the floor. In orbit it drifts, and it can end up in an astronaut's eye or in equipment. Graphite also conducts electricity, which is unwelcome near switches and circuit boards.

Then there is fire. In January 1967, a fire in the Apollo 1 cabin killed Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee during a ground test in a pure-oxygen atmosphere. Afterward NASA worked hard to remove flammable materials from spacecraft, and wood and graphite burn.

Money mattered too. In 1965 NASA had paid $128.89 each for 34 mechanical pencils, and the public outcry pushed the agency to look for something cheaper. A $2.39 pen was the cheap option.
questions.references: [Scientific American: Fact or fiction? NASA spent millions to develop a pen that would write in space (2006)](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-nasa-spen/), [Wikipedia: Apollo 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_1)

questions.title: In the joke, Soviet cosmonauts just used pencils. What did they actually do?

options.text: They used pencils at first, then bought Fisher space pens in 1969
They used pencils throughout the Soviet space program
They developed their own pressurized pen before the Americans
They used grease pencils only, because graphite was banned

questions.explanation:
Cosmonauts started with pencils, as American astronauts did. Then, a year after NASA's 1968 order, the Soviet Union ordered 100 Fisher pens and 1,000 ink cartridges for its Soyuz missions, at the same bulk discount NASA got.

That undoes the joke completely. The punchline needs the Soviets to have picked the simple solution the Americans overlooked. In fact both programs started with the "simple" solution, hit the same problems, and bought the same pen.

It's a good example of a story that survives because of its shape. A clever underdog, a wasteful giant and a one-line moral are easy to remember and fun to retell. Checking the purchase records breaks it.
questions.references: [Scientific American: Fact or fiction? NASA spent millions to develop a pen that would write in space (2006)](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-nasa-spen/)

questions.title: If you store 1 in an unsigned 8-bit integer and subtract 2, what value do you get?
questions.description: The popular *Civilization* legend depends on this calculation. Answer with a whole number.
questions.explanation:
An unsigned 8-bit integer holds 2⁸ = 256 values, from 0 to 255. There is no −1, so arithmetic that goes below 0 **wraps around** to the top, like an odometer rolling backward. 1 − 1 = 0, and one more step back lands on 255. This is called **integer underflow**, and many languages and processors behave this way for unsigned types.

A **signed** 8-bit integer uses the same 8 bits but reads them differently, covering −128 to 127. The bit pattern that means 255 unsigned means −1 signed. So in a signed variable, 1 − 2 gives −1, exactly what you'd expect.

This is the arithmetic behind the famous "Nuclear Gandhi" story. According to the legend, Gandhi's aggression in the first *Civilization* game was 1, adopting democracy subtracted 2, and the value wrapped to 255, turning the most peaceful leader into the most aggressive one. The arithmetic is right. The next Questions check whether the story is.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Integer overflow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_overflow), [Wikipedia: Nuclear Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Gandhi)

images.alt: The 256 values of an unsigned 8-bit integer drawn as a ring, with 0 at the top, 1 and 2 clockwise from it, 64 on the right, 128 at the bottom, 192 on the left, and 254 and 255 just counterclockwise of 0. An arrow goes two steps back from 1, past 0, to 255. A panel says unsigned 8-bit covers 0 to 255, so 1 − 2 = 255. A second panel says signed 8-bit covers −128 to 127 and reads the same bits as −1, so 1 − 2 = −1.
images.caption: Diagram drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: Was "Nuclear Gandhi" a real bug in the original 1991 *Civilization*?

options.text: No. Sid Meier and Civilization II's lead designer, Brian Reynolds, both say it never happened
Yes. Sid Meier confirmed it and kept it in later games as a tribute
Yes, but it was fixed in a patch before most players saw it
Nobody knows, because the original source code was lost

questions.explanation:
The people who wrote the games say no. Brian Reynolds, lead designer of *Civilization II*, said he was "99.99%" sure the bug was apocryphal. Sid Meier, who created the series, took it apart in his 2020 memoir, *Sid Meier's Memoir!*. The next Question looks at their reasons.

The story does have a real ending, which is part of why it's hard to kill. In *Civilization V* (2010), designer Jon Shafer gave Gandhi the maximum rating for building and using nuclear weapons as a deliberate joke. Players who met a nuke-happy Gandhi there took it as a knowing reference to an old bug. It was actually a reference to a myth.

When a later product nods at a legend, that's evidence that the legend was popular, not that it was true.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Nuclear Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Gandhi)

questions.title: Which of these reasons, given by the game's own designers, rule out the Nuclear Gandhi underflow in the original *Civilization*?

options.text: Integer variables in the game's C code were signed by default, so 1 − 2 gives −1, not 255
Switching to democracy didn't change an AI leader's aggression at all
The game had only three aggression levels, and Gandhi shared the lowest with about a third of the leaders
India wasn't a playable civilization in the original game
The original game had no nuclear weapons

questions.explanation:
Any one of these three reasons is enough to rule out the story.

- **The arithmetic.** In C, `int` variables are signed unless you say otherwise. Meier pointed this out in his memoir: 1 − 2 in a signed variable is −1. The wrap to 255 needs an unsigned type, and there wasn't one.
- **The cause.** Meier also wrote that the form of government didn't affect AI aggression. Democracy never subtracted 2 from anything, so there was nothing to underflow.
- **The scale.** Reynolds said there were only three aggression levels. Gandhi's lowest level wasn't special, since roughly a third of the leaders shared it. There was no scale reaching 255 for Gandhi to wrap onto.

The false Options are wrong too. India, led by Gandhi, was in the 1991 game, and so were nuclear weapons.

The myth survived because the mechanism *sounds* like real programming. Underflow is a real bug that has broken real software. A plausible mechanism is not evidence that it happened in a particular program.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Nuclear Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Gandhi), [Wikipedia: Civilization (video game)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization_(video_game))

questions.title: Where does the earliest traceable version of the Nuclear Gandhi story appear?

options.text: An unsourced 2012 edit to a TV Tropes page, about 21 years after the game came out
A list of known bugs in the original 1991 game manual
A 1990s magazine interview with Sid Meier
The patch notes for Civilization II

questions.explanation:
The earliest known version is a TV Tropes edit from 17 July 2012, which added the claim with no source. By then the first *Civilization* was over 20 years old.

It spread in 2014, after a Reddit discussion about a reposted webcomic, and a Kotaku article about Gandhi's aggression on 3 February 2014 was republished widely. From there it moved into listicles, trivia books and conference talks as an example of integer underflow.

That timeline is the tell. A bug in a 1991 game that nobody wrote about for two decades, then suddenly everybody did, points to a story that started in 2012 and not a memory from 1991. When you meet a "famous bug", look for a source from the time the software was current.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Nuclear Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Gandhi)

questions.title: In what year did operators find a moth in the Harvard Mark II computer and tape it into the logbook?
questions.explanation:
**1947**, on 9 September. The moth was trapped between the contacts of relay #70 on panel F of the Mark II, an electromechanical computer at Harvard. At 15:45 the operators removed it, taped it into the log and wrote "First actual case of bug being found."

The Mark II was built from relays: mechanical switches that clicked open and shut thousands of times. An insect caught between a relay's contacts could stop it from closing, which is a hardware fault anyone could see. Software as we think of it barely existed yet.
questions.references: [Naval History and Heritage Command: NH 96566-KN, The first "computer bug"](https://www.history.navy.mil/our-collections/photography/numerical-list-of-images/nhhc-series/nh-series/NH-96000/NH-96566-KN.html)

questions.title: This logbook page has a real moth taped to it. What does it show?

options.text: A moth found in a relay, logged as the "first actual case of bug being found": a joke, because engineers already called faults bugs
The moment the word "bug" was invented for technical faults
The first software bug, found in a program's code
Grace Hopper's personal notebook from the day she found the moth

questions.explanation:
Read the caption the operators wrote: "First **actual** case of bug being found." The word "actual" is the joke. Engineers already called faults "bugs", and here, for once, the fault was a literal insect.

The technical meaning is at least 70 years older. In an 1878 letter, Thomas Edison described how, after an invention's first flash of success, "'Bugs'—as such little faults and difficulties are called—show themselves". Webster's dictionary listed "bug" as a defect in an apparatus in 1934, well before this page.

The page doesn't show a software bug either. The moth jammed a relay, a mechanical switch. And it wasn't Grace Hopper's notebook, as the next Question explains.

Even official captions sometimes repeat the myth. The Navy's own photo record says the operators' remark introduced the term "debugging". The page itself supports only the narrower claim: a moth, a relay, and an engineer's pun.
questions.references: [Naval History and Heritage Command: NH 96566-KN, The first "computer bug"](https://www.history.navy.mil/our-collections/photography/numerical-list-of-images/nhhc-series/nh-series/NH-96000/NH-96566-KN.html), [JSTOR Daily: The bug in the computer bug story (2017)](https://daily.jstor.org/the-bug-in-the-computer-bug-story/), [Wikipedia: Software bug, history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_bug)

images.alt: A page of handwritten entries on graph paper, dated 9/9 at the top, with times down the left margin. Entries mention relays failing a speed test and a cosine tape starting. At 1545 a moth is stuck to the page with a strip of tape, next to the note "Relay #70 Panel F (moth) in relay". Below it is written "First actual case of bug being found."
images.caption: U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command photo NH 96566-KN, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:First_Computer_Bug,_1947.jpg).

questions.title: The moth is often called "Grace Hopper's bug". What was her connection to it?

options.text: She worked on the Mark II team and often told the story, but the log probably wasn't hers, and there's no evidence she found the moth
She found the moth herself and wrote the famous note
She had no connection to the Mark II and only heard about it years later
She kept the log as her private notebook and donated it to a museum

questions.explanation:
Grace Hopper was a real part of the story. She worked on the Harvard Mark II and Mark III, and in later decades she told the moth story in many talks. That retelling is why her name stuck to it.

The log itself tells a smaller story. Accounts of the day say her associates found the moth, and the Smithsonian, which holds the page, says the log book "was probably not Hopper's". The operators were the ones who wrote the joke.

This is a common pattern. The person who tells a story best becomes its hero. Hopper made major contributions of her own, including early compilers and work that led to COBOL, so crediting her with a moth she didn't find adds nothing to her record and takes something from the operators.
questions.references: [Smithsonian National Museum of American History: Log book with computer bug](https://americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_334663), [JSTOR Daily: The bug in the computer bug story (2017)](https://daily.jstor.org/the-bug-in-the-computer-bug-story/), [Wikipedia: Grace Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Hopper)

questions.title: Where is the logbook page with the moth today?

options.text: In the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History
In a display case at Harvard's Science Center
At the Computer History Museum in California
It was lost when the Mark II was scrapped

questions.explanation:
The page, moth still taped in place, belongs to the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C.

It took a detour to get there. The log stayed with the Navy, and a 1988 Navy photo record places it in the Naval Surface Warfare Center's computer museum in Dahlgren, Virginia. The Smithsonian's catalog record is also where the corrections from the previous Questions come from: the museum notes the log was probably not Hopper's and that the word "bug" was already in use.

A museum record is one of the best places to check a famous object's story, because curators document where the object came from and what it can and cannot show.
questions.references: [Smithsonian National Museum of American History: Log book with computer bug](https://americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_334663), [Naval History and Heritage Command: NH 96566-KN, The first "computer bug"](https://www.history.navy.mil/our-collections/photography/numerical-list-of-images/nhhc-series/nh-series/NH-96000/NH-96566-KN.html)

questions.title: You browse in Chrome's Incognito mode. Who may still be able to see which sites you visit?

options.text: The websites you visit
Your employer or school, if they manage the network you're on
Your internet service provider
Someone who later opens Chrome's browsing history on the same computer

questions.explanation:
Incognito mode changes what your **own browser** keeps. When you close all Incognito windows, Chrome discards the history, cookies and site data from that session. It still keeps files you downloaded and bookmarks you saved. So another person using your computer later won't find the sites in Chrome's history.

It doesn't hide your traffic from anyone else. Chrome's help page says it plainly (as of 2026): websites you visit, and organizations that manage your network, such as your school, employer or internet service provider, may be able to observe your activity. Your requests still travel over the same network, from the same IP address, to the same servers. Sites can still recognize you if you sign in.

The name suggests invisibility, but the feature is closer to "don't keep a record on this device". Every major browser's private mode works the same way.

Try it now: open an Incognito window and read the notice on the new tab page. It lists who can still see you.
questions.references: [Google Chrome Help: Browse in Incognito mode](https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/95464), [Wikipedia: Private browsing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_browsing)

questions.title: Was the QWERTY keyboard layout designed to slow typists down?

options.text: There's no good evidence for that. The layout evolved over years of prototypes, and historians still disagree about why
Yes. Christopher Sholes admitted it in his patent
Yes. Fast typists jammed the early machines, so the layout was made deliberately awkward
No. It was scientifically optimized for speed, and no layout beats it

questions.explanation:
"Designed to slow typists down" is a distorted version of one historical account, and that account is itself disputed.

- **The jamming account.** Early typewriters had typebars that could collide when neighboring keys were struck in quick succession. On this view, Christopher Sholes separated some common letter pairs to reduce jams. Even if true, the goal was fewer jams, not slower typing.
- **The telegraph account.** Koichi and Motoko Yasuoka of Kyoto University traced the layout's changes through Sholes's prototypes and argue that early users, especially telegraph operators transcribing Morse code, shaped it. On their account, the arrangement changed often and grew into QWERTY "among different requirements". A layout that slowed operators down would have been useless to people who had to keep up with an incoming message.

What both accounts agree on is that QWERTY was not planned in one step from a single principle, and neither supports a deliberate slowdown. It survives today through path dependence: once millions of people had learned it, switching cost more than any improvement was worth.

The type of evidence here is historical reconstruction from patents and prototypes. That is why the honest answer is "disputed" and not a new, equally tidy myth.
questions.references: [Smithsonian Magazine: Fact or fiction? The legend of the QWERTY keyboard (2013)](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/fact-of-fiction-the-legend-of-the-qwerty-keyboard-49863249/), [Yasuoka and Yasuoka (2011): On the prehistory of QWERTY](https://repository.kulib.kyoto-u.ac.jp/handle/2433/139379), [Wikipedia: QWERTY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QWERTY)

questions.title: Does swiping away your open iPhone apps save battery?

options.text: No. Apple says to force-close an app only if it's unresponsive, because apps in the background use little or no power
Yes. Every app in the switcher keeps running and draining the battery until you close it
Yes, but only on iPhones older than five years
No, because iOS already quits every app the moment you leave it

questions.explanation:
The app switcher shows recently used apps, not running ones. When you leave an app, iOS usually suspends it: the app stays in memory but gets no processor time, so it uses almost no power. If the system needs the memory, it quietly removes the app.

Apple's support page says it directly (as of 2026): close an app only if it's unresponsive. In 2016, a customer emailed Tim Cook to ask whether he quit his apps and whether that was necessary for battery life. Craig Federighi, Apple's head of software, replied: "No and no."

The tempting wrong answer is that iOS quits apps instantly. It doesn't. Some apps legitimately keep working in the background, such as navigation, music, calls and downloads. Those can use battery, and iOS shows you which ones in **Settings → Battery**. That list is a better guide than swiping everything away.
questions.references: [Apple Support: Close an app on your iPhone or iPod touch](https://support.apple.com/en-us/109359), [9to5Mac: Apple's software SVP says quitting multitasking apps not necessary (2016)](https://9to5mac.com/2016/03/10/should-you-quit-ios-apps-answer/)

questions.title: Final round: which of these tech stories are true?

options.text: Operators taped a real moth into a Harvard Mark II logbook in 1947
NASA once paid $128.89 each for mechanical pencils
In *Civilization V*, Gandhi was deliberately given a maximum preference for nuclear weapons, as a joke
The 404 error is named after an office at CERN
Bill Gates said in 1981 that 640K ought to be enough for anybody
NASA spent millions developing a space pen while the Soviets used pencils

questions.explanation:
Three true, three myths, and each true story sits right next to a myth.

- **The moth is real.** The page exists and is in the Smithsonian. The myth is what people add to it: that it invented the word "bug", or that it was Hopper's log.
- **The $128.89 pencils are real.** NASA bought 34 of them in 1965, and the outcry helped push it toward a cheaper option. The myth is that NASA then spent millions on a pen. Fisher paid for the pen, and NASA bought it for $2.39.
- **Civilization V's Gandhi is real.** Jon Shafer set Gandhi's nuke ratings to the maximum on purpose in 2010. The myth is the 1991 underflow bug it's taken to be referencing.
- **Room 404, the 1981 Gates quote and the millions-for-a-pen story** have no source from the time and are contradicted by the people involved or by the purchase records.

The pattern across this whole Quiz: myths rarely come from nothing. They attach to a real object, a real person or a real mechanism, then add a punchline. To separate them, ask for a source from the time the thing supposedly happened.
